extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and professional television comedy writers, sitcom writers, TV producers
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and evaluative criteria for writing, casting, and producing television comedy (especially sitcom pilots and early episodes), including character creation, joke craft, scripting practice, and production roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Casting the ideal comedic lead ('that guy')
rubrics_metrics.description: The lead actor should be a handsome, charming, self-deprecating, smart performer who can play comedy with ease and also act—someone who makes comedy look effortless and elevates material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: James Garner, Ted Danson, Alan Alda, Cary Grant. Such an actor can transform a show (e.g., imagine CHEERS without Ted Danson). Anti-pattern: scripts that lack that central, magnetic performer; actors who cannot sell subtlety or rely only on broad shtick.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acting fundamentals and honesty
rubrics_metrics.description: Acting should be grounded in professionalism and truth: be on time, know your words, hit your marks, and tell the truth; don't over-theorize acting or make it something it isn't.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoting Garner's memoir: put yourself aside and do what the writer wrote. Anti-pattern: actors who take themselves too seriously or try to 'act' rather than serve the script.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid crude character crutches (drunk character)
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't rely on an always-drunk character as the primary source of comedy; if a character must be inebriated for laughs you haven't developed them properly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: pilots where big comedy beats come only from vomiting, outrageous drunken stunts, or saying appalling things because of intoxication. Develop characters whose humor arises from personality and situation, not constant state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the man-child stereotype
rubrics_metrics.description: Steer clear of the immature, borderline brain-dead 'man-child' as a lazy comedic archetype (e.g., recurring Judd Apatow-type trope).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: characters who exist only to burp, play video games, call everyone 'bro', and rely on childish charm. Instead, create richer, fuller motivations and stakes for comedic behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the hateful mean-girl stereotype
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't default to a one-dimensional self-centered, bitchy female character as a comedy shortcut.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: female characters who are mean for cheap laughs. Make female characters layered and not merely archetypal antagonists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use pop-culture references judiciously
rubrics_metrics.description: Pop-culture name-checks can make dialogue feel authentic but overuse will date material and weaken longevity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be selective — references can help establish voice but too many will make the show age quickly. Balance authenticity with evergreen humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't substitute dripping irony for actual jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: Sardonic, ironic detachments ('Well THAT went well') are not automatic laughs; irony can't replace strong comedic writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for concrete beats, setups and punchlines, and character-derived humor rather than throwaway ironic one-liners used as a crutch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derive comedy from well-defined, real characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy should emerge from characters' desires, conflicts, quirks, and relationships rather than sketches or surface gags.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make characters 'real', consider how they relate, why they bond or clash, and what each wants. Avoid writing characters as mere sketches; dig deeper into worldview and motivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Play characters to the top of their intelligence
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters should generally be written as smarter than the joke expects; intelligence makes dialogue organically sharper and funnier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A plus when characters are intelligent — use that intelligence to craft sharper, more surprising humor. Anti-pattern: writing characters as dumb just to extract easy jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have a clear hook — why this group exists
rubrics_metrics.description: Every ensemble (especially 'friends' style shows) needs a compelling, clearly stated reason the group is together beyond 'because you say so.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the emotional/social/plot reason the ensemble is cohesive. This hook is crucial for pilots to stand out in a crowded marketplace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be demonstrably funnier — prioritize laughs
rubrics_metrics.description: In competitive spec and pilot markets, scripts must be funnier and take real effort to rise above the noise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work harder on joke craft, avoid laziness or cop-outs. If your tone trends toward irony as an excuse, question whether that's a creative choice or avoidance of comic writing work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pilot-specific allowances for exposition (overuse of names)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pilots may permissibly overuse character names to establish who everyone is; this is more acceptable in a pilot than in later episodes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use naming to orient first-time viewers, but avoid keeping that heavy-handedness in subsequent episodes where it becomes awkward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second episode strategy — reboot and retell
rubrics_metrics.description: The second episode is often harder than the pilot: it must re-establish premise for new viewers while delivering a fresh story for returning ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Over first few episodes, keep 'rebooting' premise so newcomers can jump in; be efficient (you often have two weeks to write versus months for a pilot). Practical implication: plan early episodes to both orient and advance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and value of creative consultants
rubrics_metrics.description: Creative consultants are part-time writers who come in to help with rewrites and 'pump in jokes' for produced episodes; they're not usually full-time staff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Their day typically begins with the afternoon run-through and continues through rewrite. Though studios have phased the role for cost reasons, good consultants can be invaluable for joke-heavy fixes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn and follow proper script format
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowing correct screenplay/TV script format (e.g., INT. MADISON APARTMENT – DAY) is a basic production requirement and professional expectation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New writers should read produced scripts (e.g., The Odd Couple) as templates. Formatting matters for readability and perceived professionalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place and timing of your best jokes (trailers vs film)
rubrics_metrics.description: Studios often put the sharpest, most crowd-pleasing jokes into trailers; be aware this can leave theatrical content less funny than promotional material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this observation when evaluating a script or marketing: don't judge a film's humor only by the trailer, but be mindful of where the strongest laughs are placed in a piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity in pitch/performance for commercials
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial pitch performance succeeds when the performer conveys warmth and sincerity rather than broad shtick.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: James Garner's Polaroid and beef campaigns worked because of his natural warmth. When writing or casting ad-related material, favor authenticity over caricature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Network/studio note dynamics for established shows
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful long-running shows receive more leeway from networks but still must clear significant departures from established tone/plan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you propose something very different, expect possible fights; established hits can win such fights but shouldn't expect automatic approval. Always present planned stories to network even for hits.
